entry: Steel through-arch bridge in [[Sydney]], New South Wales, Australia, spanning Sydney Harbour. Nicknamed "the Coathanger," it carries road, rail, bicycle and pedestrian traffic. Designed under John Bradfield of the New South Wales Department of Public Works and built by the British firm Dorman Long, it opened in 1932. Its design was a rough copy of the Hell Gate Bridge in [[New York City]]. At 134 m (440 ft) it is the tallest steel arch bridge. It was the world's widest long-span bridge, at 48.8 m (160 ft), until the Port Mann Bridge in [[Vancouver]] was completed in 2012.

Multi-venue performing arts center in [[Sydney]], [[New South Wales]], Australia, on Bennelong Point on Sydney Harbour. It is widely regarded as one of the world's most distinctive buildings. Danish architect Jørn Utzon designed it after winning an international competition in 1957, and an Australian team headed by Peter Hall completed it. Work was authorized in 1958, but cost and schedule overruns followed, and Utzon resigned in 1966. [[Elizabeth II|Queen Elizabeth II]] opened the building on 20 October 1973. Its roof is made of precast concrete panels, and resident companies include Opera Australia and the Sydney Symphony Orchestra. The site attracts more than ten million visitors a year. Managed by the Sydney Opera House Trust, a New South Wales government agency, it became a [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] in 2007.

American film director, producer and actor. He won two [[Academy Awards]], for Best Director and Best Picture for *Out of Africa* (1985), and was nominated for Best Director for *They Shoot Horses, Don't They?* (1969) and *Tootsie* (1982). His other films include *Jeremiah Johnson* (1972), *The Way We Were* (1973) and *Three Days of the Condor* (1975). He directed [[Robert Redford]] in seven films and acted in [[Stanley Kubrick]]'s *Eyes Wide Shut* (1999).

Metropolitan city in northeastern [[Bangladesh]] (metro pop., 2025: 1,033,000), administrative center of Sylhet District and Sylhet Division. It lies on the Surma River and is known for its tea plantations and the Ratargul Swamp Forest, one of the few freshwater swamp forests in the country. The Shah Jalal Dargah attracts thousands of pilgrims every year. Since the city's establishment in the 14th century it has been ruled by the [[Mughal Empire]], the British and the Nawabs of Bengal, and British rule under the [[East India Company]] began in the 18th century. On 12 June 1897 an earthquake demolished almost the entire town. Its tea industry, which grew from the early 20th century, and its commerce make Sylhet one of Bangladesh's most important cities after [[Dhaka]] and [[Chittagong]]. Its name is generally thought to derive from the [[Sanskrit]] Śrīhaṭṭa, the city's older name.

Basic unit of organization within a sequence of speech sounds, such as a word. Syllables are often considered the building blocks of [[Word|words]]. A syllable usually consists of a nucleus, most often a [[Vowel|vowel]], which may be preceded by an onset and followed by a coda, usually a [[Consonant|consonant]]. The word *ignite* has two syllables, *ig* and *nite*, while *dog* is a monosyllable. No precise definition of the syllable is valid for all known languages, and speakers sometimes disagree on where boundaries fall. The earliest attested syllabic writing appears on tablets from about 2800 BC in the [[Sumer|Sumerian]] city of [[Ur]], several centuries before the earliest alphabetic writing. The shift from pictographic to syllabic writing has been called "the most important advance in the history of writing." The word derives from [[Ancient Greek|Greek]] *syllabē*, meaning "taken together."

American actor and filmmaker. He rose to fame as the boxer [[Rocky]] Balboa in the *Rocky* franchise (1976–present), a role he wrote. *Rocky* (1976) earned him [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nominations for Best Actor and Best Original Screenplay. He also played the soldier John Rambo in five films beginning with *First Blood* (1982), which he co-wrote. Stallone was one of Hollywood's highest-paid actors from the mid-1980s to the late 1990s. He later played Stakar Ogord in the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]] films *Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2* and *Vol. 3*.

American poet and novelist, credited with advancing confessional poetry. Born in Jamaica Plain, [[Boston]], she studied at Smith College and, on a Fulbright scholarship, at Newnham College, [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge]]. Her works include *The Colossus and Other Poems* (1960), *Ariel* (1965) and the semi-autobiographical novel *The Bell Jar* (1963), published a month before her death. *The Collected Poems* (1981) won her a [[Pulitzer Prize]] for Poetry in 1982, a posthumous honor. She married the poet Ted Hughes in London in 1956; they had two children and separated in 1962. Plath suffered from severe depression and underwent multiple treatments with early electroconvulsive therapy. She died by [[Suicide|suicide]] in London.

Evolutionary theory, also called the endosymbiotic theory, on the origin of [[Eukaryote|eukaryotes]] from [[Prokaryote|prokaryotic]] ancestors. It holds that [[Mitochondria|mitochondria]] and [[Chloroplast|chloroplasts]] are endosymbionts descended from free-living prokaryotes that were engulfed by another prokaryote. Mitochondria appear to derive from Alphaproteobacteria, and chloroplasts from [[Cyanobacteria|cyanobacteria]]. Mitochondria and [[Plastid|plastids]] contain their own chromosomes and reproduce by binary fission, and some of these chromosomes are circular DNA like those of bacteria. The idea that chloroplasts were once independent organisms dates to the 19th century, when Andreas Schimper espoused it. The Russian botanist Konstantin Mereschkowski articulated the theory in 1905 and 1910, and Lynn Margulis substantiated it with microbiological evidence in 1967.

Close and long-term biological interaction between two organisms of different species. The term comes from [[Ancient Greek|Greek]] roots meaning "living together," and in 1879 Heinrich Anton de Bary defined it as "the living together of unlike organisms." Relationships may be obligate, with one or both partners dependent on the other, or facultative. In mutualism both partners benefit; in commensalism one benefits and the other is unaffected; in parasitism one benefits at the other's expense. Ectosymbiosis occurs on the host's surface, as with head lice, and endosymbiosis within its tissues, as with [[Algae|algae]] in reef-building corals. Symbiosis has driven evolution: mycorrhiza, insect [[Pollination|pollination]] and nitrogen-fixing bacteria in legume root nodules are major examples. [[Symbiogenesis]] is thought to have helped create [[Eukaryote|eukaryotes]] when bacteria became [[Mitochondria|mitochondria]] and [[Chloroplast|chloroplasts]].

Mark, sign or word that indicates or is understood as representing an idea, object, relationship or mathematical formula. Symbols allow people to go beyond what is known or seen by linking otherwise different concepts and experiences. All [[Communication|communication]] is achieved through symbols: a red octagon signifies "STOP," and a red rose often symbolizes love and compassion. [[Number|Numerals]] are symbols for numbers, letters may represent [[Phoneme|phonemes]], and personal names stand for individuals. In the arts, symbolism uses a concrete element to represent a more abstract idea. In [[Cartography|cartography]], an organized set of symbols forms a map's legend. The study of symbols is called [[Semiotics|semiotics]]. The English meaning "something which stands for something else" was first recorded in 1590, in [[Edmund Spenser]]'s *The Faerie Queene*.

Late 19th-century art movement of French and Belgian origin, chiefly in poetry. It sought to represent absolute truths symbolically through language and metaphorical images, largely as a reaction against [[Realism (arts)|naturalism and realism]]. Its literary origins lie in [[Charles Baudelaire]]'s *Les Fleurs du mal* (1857). Baudelaire translated [[Edgar Allan Poe]] into French, and Poe's work was a major influence. [[Stéphane Mallarmé]] and Paul Verlaine developed the aesthetic in the 1860s and 1870s. Manifestos in the 1880s attracted a generation of writers, and the critic Jean Moréas coined the term "symbolist" to distinguish the movement from the related Decadents. His Symbolist Manifesto appeared in *Le Figaro* in 1886. The movement favored spirituality, imagination and dreams, and Symbolist painting spread across the Western world in many styles.

Harmonious balance of proportion or, in mathematics, invariance of an object under transformations such as translation, reflection, rotation or scaling. An object has reflectional symmetry if a line or plane divides it into mirror images, and rotational symmetry if it can be turned about a fixed point without changing shape. Symmetries that preserve a given property of an object form a [[Group (mathematics)|group]]. In calculus, an even function is symmetric about the y-axis, and in [[Linear algebra|linear algebra]] a symmetric matrix equals its transpose. In physics, symmetry principles underlie conservation laws, as stated in [[Noether's theorem]]. In nature, bilateral symmetry predominates in animals, while [[Starfish|starfish]] show radial symmetry. In art and architecture, symmetry creates visual harmony, as in classical Greek temples and [[Islam|Islamic]] geometric designs.

Invariance of a mathematical object under a set of operations or transformations, found in many branches of mathematics. For a structured object, a symmetry is a mapping of the object onto itself that preserves its structure. For a set with no additional structure, symmetries are bijections, which give rise to [[Permutation|permutation]] groups. For points in a plane with a metric, symmetries are [[Distance|distance]]-preserving bijections called isometries. In calculus, an even function satisfies f(x) = f(−x), and an odd function has rotational symmetry about the origin. The integral of an odd function from −A to A is zero, provided it is integrable. In [[Linear algebra|linear algebra]], a symmetric matrix equals its transpose, so only square matrices can be symmetric. A real symmetric matrix represents a self-adjoint operator on a real [[Inner product space|inner product space]].

Physical or mathematical feature of a system that is preserved under some transformation. Transformations may be continuous, such as the rotation of a circle, or discrete, such as the [[Reflection (physics)|reflection]] of a bilaterally symmetric figure. Symmetries are described by [[Group theory|symmetry groups]], and they can simplify problems and explain conservation laws. [[Speed of light|The speed of light]] is the same in all frames of reference, a symmetry described in [[Special relativity]] by the Poincaré group. Other examples include the invariance of physical laws under coordinate changes in [[General relativity]] and the gauge invariances of [[Electromagnetism]] and the [[Standard Model]]. Symmetries may be global, applied the same way at every point of [[Spacetime|spacetime]], or local, applied differently at each point.

Symphony in C minor by [[Gustav Mahler]], nicknamed the *Resurrection* Symphony. Mahler wrote its first movement in 1888 as a single-movement symphonic poem, *Totenfeier* (Funeral Rites), and finished the work in 1894. The finale uses Friedrich Gottlieb Klopstock's hymn "Die Auferstehung" (The Resurrection), which Mahler heard at the 1894 funeral of the conductor Hans von Bülow. Like [[Symphony No. 9 (Beethoven)|Beethoven's Ninth]], it uses a chorus in its final movement. It is scored for large orchestra, including [[Trumpet|trumpets]], [[Trombone|trombones]] and a [[Tuba|tuba]], plus vocal soloists and a mixed chorus. It was first performed in 1895 and was among Mahler's most successful works during his lifetime. A performance usually lasts 80 to 90 minutes, and a BBC Music Magazine survey of conductors ranked it the fifth-greatest symphony of all time.

Symphony in E♭ major, Op. 55, by [[Ludwig van Beethoven]], known as the *Eroica*. Composed mainly in 1803–1804, it has four movements and typically lasts 45 to 55 minutes. It broke with earlier symphonic conventions in form, length, harmony and emotional content, and is widely considered a landmark in the transition from the Classical to the Romantic era. It is often considered the first Romantic symphony. Beethoven first conducted a private performance on 9 June 1804, and the first public performance followed on 7 April 1805 in [[Vienna]]. The work was originally dedicated to [[Napoleon]], but Beethoven removed the dedication after Napoleon proclaimed himself emperor, and it was rededicated to Prince Franz Joseph von Lobkowitz. Its second movement is a [[Funeral|funeral march]].

Symphony in C major, K. 551, by [[Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart]], nicknamed the *Jupiter*. Mozart completed it on 10 August 1788. It is the longest and last symphony he composed, and many critics regard it as among the greatest in classical music. The nickname was probably coined by the impresario Johann Peter Salomon. It was the last of three symphonies Mozart wrote in rapid succession in the summer of 1788. Unlike the earlier No. 39, it has no introduction but a grand finale. The autograph manuscript is preserved in the Berlin State Library. The four movements follow the traditional Classical symphonic form, and the work typically lasts about 33 minutes.

Symphony in C minor, Op. 67, by [[Ludwig van Beethoven]], one of the best-known symphonies. Its distinctive opening motif, "short-short-short-long," is often described as fate knocking at the door. Beethoven wrote it between 1804 and 1808, a period marked by the [[Napoleonic Wars]] and by Napoleon's troops occupying Vienna in 1805. It was first performed in Vienna on 22 December 1808 in a concert that lasted more than four hours. The critic E. T. A. Hoffmann called it "one of the most important works of the time." It was dedicated to Prince Joseph Franz von Lobkowitz and Count Razumovsky. It was Beethoven's first symphony to use [[Trombone|trombones]].

Choral symphony in D minor, Op. 125, by [[Ludwig van Beethoven]], his final complete symphony. Composed between 1822 and 1824, it was first performed in [[Vienna]] on 7 May 1824. It was the first symphony by a major composer to use vocal parts. Its fourth movement sets an adapted text of [[Friedrich Schiller]]'s poem "An die Freude" (Ode to Joy) for four vocal soloists and a [[Choir|chorus]]. An instrumental arrangement of the chorus was adopted by the [[Council of Europe]] and later the [[European Union]] as the anthem of Europe. In 2001 [[UNESCO]] added Beethoven's handwritten score to its Memory of the World Register, the first musical score so designated. Many critics regard it as one of the supreme achievements in the history of music.

Extended musical composition in Western classical music, most often for orchestra. The word comes from ancient Greek *symphōnía*, meaning "agreement or concord of sound." By the late 18th century it denoted a work of several distinct movements, often three or four, the first usually in sonata form. Symphonies are almost always scored for strings, brass, woodwinds and percussion, involving about 30 to 100 musicians. Some include voices, as in Beethoven's Ninth and [[Gustav Mahler]]'s Second. The direct forerunner was the three-movement Italian overture, or *sinfonia*, of Baroque opera. [[Joseph Haydn]], often called the father of the symphony, composed 104 of them. [[Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart]] and [[Ludwig van Beethoven]] further developed the form, and Romantic composers such as [[Robert Schumann]] and [[Johannes Brahms]] expanded it.

Medical therapy that relieves the symptoms of a disease without affecting its underlying cause. Also called supportive or palliative treatment, it aims at the comfort and well-being of the patient. For many diseases, including most viral illnesses such as [[Influenza]] and Rift Valley fever, it is the only treatment available. Examples include [[Analgesic|analgesics]] for pain, anti-inflammatory agents for arthritis, antitussives for cough and antipyretics for fever. It can be dangerous when it masks an underlying condition: low-grade fever lasting 15 days or more may be the only sign of staphylococcus bacteremia, and suppressing it can delay [[Antibiotic|antibiotic]] treatment. Symptomatic treatment also carries its own risks, such as stomach [[Bleeding|bleeding]] and [[Central nervous system|central nervous system]] effects.

Place of worship for [[Jews]] or Samaritans, also called a *shul* (from [[Yiddish]] for "school") or a temple. The Hebrew name *beit knesset* means "house of assembly." A synagogue has a main sanctuary with an ark where the [[Torah]] scrolls are kept, a platform called the *bema* in front of it, and raised galleries for women. Services include daily and Sabbath prayers, weddings, and bar and bat mitzvahs, and many synagogues also have study rooms, classrooms and social halls. [[Halakha|Jewish law]] allows communal worship wherever a minyan of at least 10 Jewish adults is assembled, so a synagogue building is not essential for worship. A synagogue does not replace the long-destroyed [[Temple]] in [[Jerusalem]]. Its origins are obscure, and scholars have proposed several theories.

Clade of tetrapod vertebrates that includes all [[Mammal|mammals]] and their extinct relatives. It is one of the two major clades of amniotes, the other being Sauropsida, which includes all living reptiles and birds. Synapsids have a single lower temporal opening in the skull behind each eye socket, which allowed larger jaw muscles and a more efficient bite. The earliest synapsids appeared in the [[Carboniferous]] period, about 315 to 307 million years ago. They were the largest terrestrial vertebrates in the [[Permian]] period, and [[Dimetrodon]] was among the apex predators. Synapsid diversity was severely reduced by the [[Permian–Triassic extinction event]], and only two groups of therapsids survived into the Triassic. The cynodont lineage that includes mammals was the only synapsid group to survive beyond the Triassic. After the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event]] wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs, mammals rose to dominance in the [[Cenozoic]], with roughly 6,800 species living today.

Combining or merging of distinct beliefs or schools of thought, particularly religious ones. In religion, syncretism blends two or more belief systems into a new one, or absorbs beliefs from unrelated traditions. It often results from contact between cultures or from conquest, when conquerors bring their beliefs but do not wholly eradicate older ones. The Hellenistic god Serapis combined attributes of [[Zeus]] and [[Osiris]] to promote unity in the Ptolemaic kingdom. Adherents of [[Abrahamic religions|revealed religions]] often regard syncretism as a betrayal of their faith, and critics may use the term as a disparaging epithet. The English word is first attested in 1618, derived from Modern Latin. A popular etymology, from a "Cretan federation" mentioned by [[Plutarch]], is spurious.

Set of medical signs and symptoms that are correlated with each other and often associated with a particular disease or disorder. The word comes from the Greek for "concurrence." When a syndrome has a definite cause, it becomes a disease, though the terms are often used interchangeably. [[Down syndrome]] has a known pathogenesis, toxic shock syndrome can result from various toxins, and premenstrual syndrome is a set of symptoms rather than a disease. Many syndromes are named after the physicians who described them, although descriptive names are now preferred. Early physicians recognized syndromes by their symptoms, as in [[Avicenna]]'s *The Canon of Medicine* (1025), which describes diagnosing pleurisy this way. Infectious syndromes such as [[Encephalitis]] and [[Hepatitis]] can have several causes.
